newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia still cautious on Pol Pot surrender.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia still cautious on Pol Pot surrender.

text.p: Cambodian government officials were unable to confirm on Thursday a day-old Khmer Rouge radio report that despised guerrilla strongman Pol Pot had surrendered to former comrades-in-arms turned enemies.
"I can't say I believe it or don't believe it," Defence Minister Tea Banh told Reuters. "I'll believe it if I see him".
Secretary of State for Defence Ek Sereywath said the report could not yet be confirmed.
"I've heard about this but I can't confirm it. The news is very complicated," he said.

Clandestine Khmer Rouge radio, apparently controlled by a rival rebel faction that has broken with the notorious leader of Cambodia's notorious 1975-79 "killing fields" regime, reported on Wednesday that Pol Pot surrendered to former comrades.
The radio gave no further details about his location or his fate, saying only he had turned himself in to "confess".
The broadcast was repeated on Thursday morning, but without any fresh information.

Cambodia's First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said last week that the Khmer Rouge had split and most of Pol Pot's supporters had turned against him after the guerrilla leader executed his defence chief and family members.
Ranariddh said Pol Pot and a small group of loyalists were on the run in northern Cambodia, holding senior Khmer Rouge leader Khieu Sampan and others hostage.
Ranariddh was not available for comment on Thursday, but an aide said the prince welcomed the news of Pol Pot's surrender if it turned out to be true.
"If it is true it's good for the whole country," said Kong Vibol, deputy chief of Ranariddh's cabinet.
"The result is great for the whole naton but first he must give up all materiel, military materiel, weapons, to the royal government," he said.
"He will have to face trial, an international court for genocide," Kong Vibol said. Cambodia's Second Prime Minster Hun Sen also reacted with scepticism to the guerrilla radio report.
"We must be careful about this," Hun Sen told Reuters late on Wednesday. "This is not normal. Everything is still a mystery."
The Khmer Rouge government led by Pol Pot was responsible for the deaths of more than a million Cambodians through executions, torture, disease, starvation and overwork.
Phnom Penh itself was quiet on Wednesday night, a day after security men loyal to the two premiers clashed in the city centre.
Two of Ranariddh's bodyguards were killed in the 90-minute battle on Tuesday night.
The two co-premiers have for months been locked in a bitter feud over power-sharing in their coalition government.
